topicSummary: The Two Pointers technique is an optimization strategy used to iterate through linear data structures like arrays or linked lists using two distinct reference points simultaneously, often reducing time complexity from O(N^2) to O(N).
learningObjectives: Identify problems suitable for two pointer optimization over nested loops
Distinguish between opposite-directional (collision) and equi-directional (fast/slow) pointer patterns
Analyze the time and space complexity benefits of in-place pointer manipulation
prerequisites: Array and Linked List data structures

coreConcepts.name: Opposite-Directional Pointers
coreConcepts.explanation: One pointer starts at the beginning and the other at the end, moving toward each other until they meet or satisfy a condition.
coreConcepts.importance: Crucial for processing sorted arrays (e.g., Two Sum II) or checking palindromes.

coreConcepts.name: Equi-Directional (Fast & Slow) Pointers
coreConcepts.explanation: Both pointers start at the beginning, but one moves faster than the other.
coreConcepts.importance: Standard approach for cycle detection (Floyd's Cycle-Finding) or finding the middle of a linked list.

coreConcepts.name: In-Place Swapping
coreConcepts.explanation: Using pointers to swap elements directly within the existing data structure to minimize space usage.
coreConcepts.importance: Allows for O(1) space complexity algorithms.

commonMisconceptions: Assuming the input array must always be sorted for any two-pointer approach (required for binary search logic, but not for partitioning or cycle detection)
Confusing the two pointers technique strictly with the sliding window technique (sliding window focuses on a specific sub-array size/sum, while two pointers focuses on distinct indices)
realWorldIntuition: Two people organizing a messy bookshelf: one person stands at the left end and one at the right. They check items simultaneously and swap books to their correct sides without needing a second empty shelf.
recommendedFlow: Define the inefficiency of nested loops (brute force)
Introduce the concept of using two independent indices
Explain the 'Opposite Ends' pattern with a sorted array example
Explain the 'Fast and Slow' pattern with a cycle detection example
